summary: Fox News Digital interviews Pastor Jesse Bradley of Grace Community Church in Auburn, Washington, who argues that 'In God We Trust' remains essential as surveys show America becoming less religious and more secular. The article traces the phrase's history from the Civil War, coinage and the 1956 motto designation to its constitutional standing and a 2011 congressional reaffirmation. Bradley says real trust in God must be lived daily, not just stated on currency.
one_line: Washington pastor Jesse Bradley says 'In God We Trust' is vital as American faith wanes, while the article reviews the motto's history and legal standing.
key_facts: Pastor Jesse Bradley of Grace Community Church in Auburn, Washington, near Seattle, spoke to Fox News Digital about America's relationship with God.
'In God We Trust' has been an official statement of national faith since the Civil War and the official U.S. motto since 1956.
The phrase first appeared on U.S. Mint coins in 1865, at the end of the Civil War.
'In God We Trust' was added to paper currency in 1957, after it became the official national motto.
The U.S. Congress voted to reaffirm 'In God We Trust' as the national motto by 396-6 in 2011.
The motto on currency has been deemed constitutional in numerous rulings by the Supreme Court and lower courts.
Psalm 56:11 states: 'In God have I put my trust; I will not be afraid what man can do unto me,' and a substantially similar phrase appears in the Quran.
Some reports say Pennsylvania troops used the phrase in the American Revolution and again in the Civil War.
Francis Scott Key's final stanza of the poem that became the National Anthem includes 'in God is our trust.'
Bradley said, 'We can't compartmentalize God into one day, hour or place,' calling the relationship with God '24-7.'
Bradley said America has created idols and forsaken 'living water,' citing idolatry, materialism, pride and hatred.
Bradley said, 'I believe we are at a crossroads spiritually,' and that trust matters most when written 'on our hearts,' not just on currency.
Bradley said the motto 'doesn't nullify the freedom to choose faith. Nothing is forced.'
The article says false idols of celebrity, technology and government appear to have replaced trust in God in recent decades.
